method: An in-house estimate for 2025. The United States column is based on SIA and BCG's measurement of EDA and core IP together. That measurement was 74 percent American and 20 percent European in 2019 (2021 report, Exhibit 14) and 68 and 25 in 2022 (2024 report, Exhibit 2). The EDA-only split then comes from the two American vendors' filed revenue: $4.37bn of EDA product-group revenue at Synopsys in FY2025 (62.0 percent of $7,054.2m) and $3.71bn of Core EDA at Cadence (70 percent of $5,296.8m). Each firm counts under its parent company's home country, so Siemens EDA, run from Oregon but owned by Germany's Siemens AG, sits in the DE column.
note: Firm shares converted to country by parent-company headquarters. Synopsys and Cadence, both American, hold roughly seven-tenths of the EDA tool revenue the row counts. Synopsys had $7,054.2m of total revenue in FY2025, of which the EDA product group was 62.0 percent, Design IP 24.8 and the newly acquired Ansys 10.7. Cadence had $5,296.8m of total revenue in FY2025, of which Core EDA was 70 percent. Keysight EDA and PDF Solutions add to the US column. The largest judgment call is Siemens EDA, the former Mentor Graphics. It is run from Wilsonville, Oregon, but owned by Siemens AG, so the row assigns it to DE under the same parent-company rule that puts Zeiss in DE. The supplier list counts each firm by its own headquarters and so places Siemens EDA in the US. Assigning it to the US instead would put the US near 87 percent and drop DE to about 1. Siemens does not disclose EDA revenue separately in its annual report. That gap makes the German column the least certain number in the row, and it is the reason the row is an estimate. SemiAnalysis estimated in May 2026 that Siemens EDA had $2.2bn to $2.5bn of revenue in 2025, in an industry it sized at $18bn including design IP. JP is Zuken plus Altium, which Renesas acquired in 2024. CN is Empyrean, Primarius, Semitronix and X-Epic, which still focus on analog and packaging tools and lack a full digital flow, the complete chain of tools needed to design a digital chip. The row excludes design IP, which is counted separately under Core IP. ETO's documentation says it counts each firm under the country where its ultimate parent has its headquarters. Its provider table still lists Mentor Graphics, which Siemens bought in 2017, under the United States. CSET's own 2019 figure, carried as node N84 in ETO's provision table, puts the United States at 96 percent and gives Germany no share.
trend: Concentration has been static since 2021, except that China's share roughly tripled from a tiny base. The rise came after the United States required an export license for design-software sales to China from May to July 2025, which pushed Chinese buyers toward Empyrean and its peers.

method: An in-house estimate for 2025, built from the design-IP licensing and royalty revenue the largest vendors file (Arm $4,920m in the year to March 2026, Synopsys $1,752m of Design IP in FY2025, Cadence about $742m, or 14 percent of revenue). It updates CSET's 2019 split of the segment, carried as node N85 in ETO's provision table, which was US 52, GB 43, CN 2, TW 1 on a $3.9bn market. The denominator is an estimate, because Imagination, SiFive and the Chinese vendors publish nothing comparable. SEMI's ESD Alliance counted $7.87bn of semiconductor IP revenue in 2025, the sum of its four quarterly reports. It does not name the firms it counts. If Arm is among them, Arm's revenue for the year to March 2026 would be more than three-fifths of that total, above the 48 percent in this estimate.
note: GB is Arm, based in Cambridge, with revenue of $4,920m in the year to March 2026, of which royalties were $2,613m. Arm is majority-owned by SoftBank of Japan, so a split by ownership would move those 48 points from GB to JP. US is Synopsys IP, Cadence IP, Rambus, SiFive and Ceva. Alphawave moves from GB to the US column with Qualcomm's acquisition, announced in 2025. CN is VeriSilicon and the Chinese vendors of designs based on RISC-V, an open processor instruction set that needs no license. TW is eMemory. Other is Imagination Technologies and smaller vendors. Shares are of design-IP licensing and royalty revenue and do not count chips shipped using the IP. The row is an estimate because the four vendors that file public accounts cover about four-fifths of it, and the rest comes from private firms.
trend: The UK-US duopoly has been broadly stable since 2021. RISC-V designs have taken a small amount of business from Arm, and Chinese IP vendors' share has grown from about 2 percent to about 5 percent.

method: Country shares of the silicon wafer market published by Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry in December 2025, from Fuji Keizai's semiconductor materials survey, on a headquarters basis. Japan's 53 percent is printed on the chart. The other columns are measured from the exact bar shapes stored in the PDF. Those measurements reproduce every printed label on the slide exactly and sum to 100.
note: Polished and epitaxial silicon wafers for semiconductor use, by revenue and by parent-company headquarters. An epitaxial wafer is a polished wafer with an extra layer of crystal grown on top. JP is Shin-Etsu Handotai and SUMCO, TW is GlobalWafers and KR is SK Siltron. DE is Siltronic, and it carries the source's whole European column, which also includes Finland's Okmetic, owned by China's National Silicon Industry Group (NSIG). The US column is zero because no meaningful merchant wafer supplier, one that sells its wafers to chipmakers, is headquartered in the US. Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, Siltronic and GlobalWafers all operate US plants, but the row counts them by headquarters. The source publishes no China column for either 2021 or 2023, so Zing Semiconductor, NSIG, Simgui, TCL Zhonghuan and Gritek sit inside the five-point Other column. CSET put China under 5 percent of wafers in 2019, and under 1 percent of 300 mm wafers. Eswin, the largest Chinese maker of 300 mm wafers, says in its October 2025 prospectus that it alone had about 6 percent of global 300 mm shipments in 2024. It also says it had about 7 percent of capacity at the end of that year. Its 2026 half-year report puts its share of shipments at about 7.7 percent in the first half of 2026. Siltronic's 2025 annual report says the five largest makers, itself included, meet roughly 75 percent of global demand, on a measure it does not define. That leaves more room for other suppliers than the five-point Other column does. CSET's 2019 split, carried as node N26 in ETO's provision table, was JP 56, TW 16, DE 14, KR 10, CN 4 on a $10.9bn market. So since 2019, Japanese and German share has gone to Taiwan and Korea. SEMI put silicon wafer revenue at $11.4bn in 2025.
trend: Shares barely moved on this measure between the source's 2021 and 2023 figures. Japan went from 52 percent to 53 as printed, Korea from 13.1 to 13.0 and Europe from 10.3 to 10.0, and Taiwan held at 19.0. The change is in the older, smaller wafer sizes and inside the Other column, where the Chinese 300 mm entrants sit. CSET had China under 5 percent in 2019 and under 1 percent of 300 mm wafers. Eswin alone had about 6 percent of global 300 mm shipments in 2024 and about 7.7 percent in the first half of 2026.

method: Country shares of the photoresist market published by Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry in December 2025, from Fuji Keizai's semiconductor materials survey, on a headquarters basis. Japan's 78 percent is printed on the chart and is used as printed. The other columns are measured from the exact bar shapes stored in the PDF, and those measurements reproduce every printed label on the slide exactly. With Japan as printed and the rest measured, the row sums to 99.6.
note: Japanese companies, among them JSR, Tokyo Ohka Kogyo, Shin-Etsu Chemical, Sumitomo Chemical and Fujifilm, held 78 percent of photoresist revenue in 2023 on METI's count by company nationality. They held a materially higher share of EUV resist, where Japan is close to a monopoly and where CSET found China has nothing at all. US is DuPont, Merck's US-based EMD Electronics business and Inpria, a pre-commercial maker of metal-oxide resist. The source shows no separate European column. KR is Dongjin Semichem and SK Materials Performance. The Chinese suppliers, Kempur, Nata and Jingrui, sit in the 2.4-point Other column and serve mostly i-line and KrF grades, the resists for older, longer-wavelength lithography. CSET put China under 5 percent of a $3.3bn photoresist market in 2019. The state-backed Japan Investment Corporation took JSR private in 2024. That makes Japan's position in photoresist a policy tool as well as a commercial one. CSET states that Japan dominates photoresist with 90 percent of the market on 2019 data, a figure on a narrower base and six years older than this one.
trend: METI prints Japan at 77 percent in 2021 and 78 in 2023 on the same measure, so Japan's share of photoresist as a whole is not falling. Korea rose from 4.2 to 6.4 over the same two years, and the unattributed Other column, where the Chinese suppliers sit, fell from 5.7 to 2.4. Chinese and Korean firms have had resists for older chip generations (mature nodes) approved by chipmakers, but EUV resist remains Japanese.

method: An in-house model, because no allowed source splits electronic gases by country as a category. The shares start from the suppliers CSET lists for the segment, a $6bn market in 2019 that CSET sources to SEMI. The model weights each firm by the size of its electronic-gas business and checks the result against the country shares for individual gases that METI published in December 2025. Each firm counts under its parent company's home country except Linde, which the row counts under DE for its operating history although the supplier list places it in the UK.
note: Electronic specialty and bulk gases for fabs. The row's weakness is that it mixes the bulk industrial gases, where Linde, Air Liquide and Air Products dominate, with the specialty molecules, where Japan and Korea dominate. Firm-to-country mapping: JP is Nippon Sanso Holdings/Taiyo Nippon Sanso, Resonac (formerly Showa Denko) and Kanto Denka, which lead in fluorinated etch gases. DE is Linde and Merck. Linde plc, formed by the merger of Praxair and Linde AG, is incorporated in Ireland, with principal executive offices in the UK and the US, and the supplier list places it in the UK by headquarters. The row counts Linde under DE because of its operating history, and ETO's provider table also lists Linde under Germany. That call could be argued either way. EU-other is Air Liquide of France. US is Air Products and Entegris. KR is SK Specialty and Wonik. CN is Huate Gas, Jinhong Gas and PERIC. For the molecules used in etch and clean, the Japanese column understates Japan by a wide margin, and the row understates China's position. METI, publishing Fuji Keizai's 2023 survey, puts Japan at 92 percent of fluorine gas mixtures, 97 of carbonyl sulfide, 77 of hydrogen bromide, 72 of hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) etch gases, 65 of chlorine gases and 61 of perfluorocarbon (PFC) etch gases. In the same survey Korea holds 47 percent of nitrogen trifluoride, and China holds 24 percent of it and 13 percent of HFC etch gases. China also supplies most of the world's rare gases, a position that strengthened after Ukrainian neon production stopped in 2022. Specialty gases are the least well-measured segment in the matrix, because CSET names the suppliers and the market size but publishes no shares.
trend: China's share has risen since 2021, as Chinese suppliers replaced Ukrainian and Russian rare gases and moved into higher-value fluorinated gases.

method: Node N20 in ETO's provision table: CSET's analysis of TechInsights 2025 data on a $13bn market, published in July 2026. ASML is the only supplier, so the country column is the firm column.
note: ASML is the sole supplier, on a 2025 market of about $13bn. ASML's annual report records revenue from 48 EUV systems in 2025 (four EXE and 44 NXE), out of 535 systems sold. The 100 percent figure counts the vendor's headquarters and hides where the parts are made. Carl Zeiss SMT (DE) makes the projection and illumination optics and is the only firm that can. Trumpf (DE) makes the CO2 drive lasers, and Cymer (US, San Diego, an ASML subsidiary) makes the light sources. In 2025 ASML bought €4.4bn from Zeiss alone across its whole business, more than a quarter of the €16.2bn it spent with all its suppliers. China has no EUV tool and no credible near-term path to one. Its published work has not gone beyond research and a laser-discharge-plasma light source. The underlying market shares are TechInsights', relayed by CSET.
trend: Unchanged at 100 percent since the technology shipped. The only change is a higher value per tool, as ASML adds its newer and costlier High-NA EXE:5200 systems to its sales.

method: The row weights the three DUV nodes in ETO's provision table by their stated 2025 market sizes: ArF immersion ($11.7bn, ASML 99.3 percent, N22), ArF dry ($508m, ASML 94.4, N21) and KrF ($1.7bn, ASML 66, N105). Across the $13.9bn combined market, that gives NL 95.1 and JP 4.9. The underlying shares are TechInsights' data, analyzed by CSET.
note: Revenue-weighted across the three DUV classes in the CSET/ETO 2025 data. In ArF immersion ($11.7bn), ASML had 99.3 percent, and the source leaves the other 0.7 with Japan without naming a firm. In ArF dry ($0.51bn), ASML had 94.4 and Nikon 5.6. In KrF ($1.7bn), ASML had 66, and the other 34 is mostly Canon and Nikon. ASML's own 2025 figures are consistent: 131 ArF immersion systems for EUR 10,311m, 16 ArF dry for EUR 427m and 78 KrF for EUR 1,001m. The row excludes i-line tools, an older type that is not DUV and where Canon leads with 53.7 percent. Including i-line would roughly double Japan's share of the wider optical-lithography market. China's SMEE does not show up in DUV revenue. Its best delivered tool remains a 90 nm-class scanner without immersion, and its 28 nm-class ArF immersion scanner is still in development.
trend: ASML's DUV share has held near 95 percent since 2021. China's share of ASML's net system sales fell from 41 percent in 2024 to 33 percent in 2025.

method: Node N36 in ETO's provision table: CSET's analysis of TechInsights 2025 data on a $26.2bn market, published in July 2026. The source's Swiss and British columns are grouped here into Other and its French column into EU-other. Every other column is as published.
note: Covers chemical and physical vapor deposition (CVD, PVD), atomic layer deposition (ALD), epitaxy and electrochemical plating for front-end wafer processing. Firm-to-country mapping: US is Applied Materials (41.2 points on its own), Lam Research (16.9) and Veeco (1.3). JP is Tokyo Electron (9.7) and Kokusai Electric (3.3). NL is ASM International (10.9), which leads ALD. CN is NAURA (6.3) and Piotech (2.6). KR is Wonik IPS and Jusung, and Other is mostly Swiss and UK suppliers. The shares are TechInsights' measurement, relayed by CSET.
trend: China's share rose from 2 percent in 2019 to 7 percent in 2024 on CSET's earlier count. This row's 2025 data puts it at 9.8 percent, among the largest Chinese gains in the equipment chain.

method: Node N55 in ETO's provision table: CSET's analysis of TechInsights 2025 data on a $29.1bn etch-and-clean market, published in July 2026. The source's 'various countries' column is carried here as Other.
note: Firm-to-country mapping: US is Lam Research (36.7 points), Applied Materials (12.7) and ACM Research (2.4). ACM Research is US-listed but operates mainly through its Shanghai subsidiary, so it arguably belongs partly in the CN column. JP is Tokyo Electron (22.1), SCREEN Holdings (7.8) and Hitachi High-Tech (1.7) on the clean side. CN is NAURA (5.2) and AMEC (4.4). CSIS reports that Chinese tool vendors already hold about 40 percent of China's own etch and thin-film deposition market, which matters more than their global share. The shares are TechInsights' measurement, relayed by CSET.
trend: China's share rose from under 3 percent in 2019 to almost 9 percent in 2024 on CSET's earlier count, and to 10.1 percent in 2025. AMEC is the clearest case of a Chinese tool vendor competing on equal terms with foreign vendors at mature nodes, the older chip generations.

method: Node N60 in ETO's provision table: CSET's analysis of TechInsights 2025 process-control data on a $15.7bn market, published in July 2026. The source's Hungarian column is carried here as EU-other and its 'various countries' column as Other.
note: Firm-to-country mapping: US is KLA (56.8 points, over half the market on its own), Applied Materials (11.2) and Onto Innovation (2.6). JP is Lasertec (6.4), Hitachi High-Tech (6.2) and Rigaku (1.2). NL is ASML's YieldStar overlay and metrology line (5.9). Overlay is how well each patterned layer lines up with the one below. IL is Nova (4.3) and Camtek (1.6), EU-other is Hungary and DE is Carl Zeiss AIMS mask metrology. Two chokepoints do not show at this level of detail. Lasertec holds effectively all actinic EUV mask-blank inspection, which checks blank masks using EUV light itself. Zeiss holds all AIMS EUV aerial-image mask review, which checks how a finished mask's pattern will print. The shares are TechInsights' measurement, relayed by CSET.
trend: Metrology and inspection is the most durable US position in the chain. China held 0.7 percent globally in 2025 on CSET's count, though Skyverse (Shenzhen Zhongke Feice) reported 2025 revenue up 48.75 percent on 2024.

method: CSET's 2019 country split for photomasks, carried as node N33 in ETO's provision table, is Japan 53, the United States 40 and Taiwan 7 on a roughly $4bn market. It counts chipmakers' own captive mask shops alongside merchant suppliers. CSET built it from company financial statements.
note: The photomask split is the oldest figure in the matrix and the weakest. The US share is high because the split counts captive mask shops alongside merchants. Intel's and GlobalFoundries' in-house mask operations sit in the US column, TSMC's in TW and Samsung's in KR. Captive shops held 66 percent of photomask revenue in 2025 on SEMI's count, as relayed by Photronics. JP is Toppan (renamed Tekscend in 2024), Dai Nippon Printing and Hoya. METI's December 2025 slide, from Fuji Keizai's survey, gives a newer split by company headquarters for 2023. It prints Japan at 19 percent. Measured off the chart, the United States is about 11 percent and Taiwan about 2, with about 68 percent in an Other column that the slide does not break down. That Other column is close to the 63 percent captive share SEMI counted for 2023, so the two splits cannot be compared column by column. Since 2019 the total market has grown above $5bn, captive share has stayed near two-thirds, and Photronics has added US, Taiwan and China capacity. Hoya has also become the acute chokepoint in EUV mask blanks, the coated glass plates that EUV masks are patterned on. That dependency does not appear in a revenue split at all. Hoya's own estimate for the year to March 2026, drawn as a pie chart without numbers, shows it with about four-fifths of that market and a single rival with the rest. The country columns are indicative only, and date from 2019.
trend: Japanese mask-blank suppliers have strengthened at the leading edge since 2021. On SEMI's count the captive share of mask revenue went from 65 percent in 2021 to 63 percent in 2022 through 2024 and 66 percent in 2025.

method: Logic wafer fabrication capacity below 10 nm by fab location in 2022, from SIA and BCG's 2024 report (Exhibit 6). The report draws on Department of Commerce and SEMI data. It counts fabs that start 5,000 or more wafers a month on wafers 8 inches or larger, and leaves out R&D fabs.
note: The row counts capacity by fab location, wherever the company is headquartered. Fab location is where the physical risk lies. In 2022 all of it was in Taiwan and South Korea, and the United States, Japan, Europe and China held none. TSMC's Arizona fab runs its 4 nm-class N4 process and Intel makes chips on its 18A process in Arizona, so the US column is no longer zero. But no allowed source publishes a newer split by node. SemiAnalysis put Taiwan's share of the world's advanced-node capacity at over 90 percent in December 2025, without tying the term to a node size or giving other countries' shares. Epoch AI assumed in March 2026 that TSMC alone does about 90 percent of the world's advanced-node fabrication. That is a share by company, used as a model input, so it counts TSMC's Arizona output with its Taiwan fabs and cannot replace the 2022 split by fab location.
trend: SIA and BCG project Taiwan's share to fall from 69 percent in 2022 to 47 percent in 2032 and the US share to rise from zero to 28 percent.

method: Logic wafer fabrication capacity at 28 nm and above by fab location in 2022, from SIA and BCG's 2024 report (Exhibit 6), on the same fab definition as the leading-edge row. Columns sum to 99 because of rounding in the source, and the source's Europe column is carried as EU-other.
note: Capacity by fab location. The source's Other column covers Malaysia, Singapore, India and the rest of the world. In a February 2025 filing SIA counted every type of chip made at 28 nm and above, memory and analog included. It put China at 33 percent of that capacity in 2023, up from 19 percent in 2015. That definition is broader than this row's logic-only measure, so the two figures are not directly comparable.
trend: SIA and BCG project China's share to rise from 33 percent in 2022 to 37 percent in 2032, while Taiwan's falls from 30 to 25 percent.

method: Firm shares printed in SK hynix's Form 424B4 prospectus of July 2026 (SK hynix 34.8, Samsung 34.5, Micron 23.5, Others 7.3 for 2025), summed to country by parent-company headquarters. The prospectus attributes the figures to IDC, Worldwide Memory Market Shares.
note: The figures are IDC's, adopted by SK hynix in a registered prospectus, a company filing that carries securities-law liability. The shares are of revenue, and a count of memory bits shipped would give a different picture. Prices spiked in 2025, so a revenue share says as much about pricing as about who can make what. The split is also by headquarters. Micron makes most of its bits in Taiwan and Japan, so a split by production site would move them. The source does not name the firms in 'Others', but that column holds China's CXMT and Taiwan's Nanya, Winbond and PSMC. It grew from 5.1 in 2024 to 7.3 in 2025 and 9.9 in the first quarter of 2026, the fastest-moving number in the row.
trend: SK hynix passed Samsung for the first time in 2025 on the strength of HBM, then fell back behind it in the first quarter of 2026. The longer-term change is in the 'Others' column, which has nearly doubled since 2024. SemiAnalysis models CXMT at 9 percent of global DRAM bit shipments in 2025, rising to 12 percent by 2027. Those bits are in DDR4, an older generation of DRAM, and in consumer parts. AI buyers compete instead for server DDR5 and HBM.

method: Firm shares printed in the same SK hynix Form 424B4 prospectus (SK hynix 63.2, Samsung 19.3, Micron 17.4 for 2025), summed to country by parent-company headquarters. Columns sum to 99.9 because of rounding in the source. The prospectus attributes the figures to IDC.
note: There is no fourth supplier and no Chinese column at all. The prospectus's figures for other periods also show how fast the ranking moves as suppliers pass or fail customers' qualification tests. In 2024 the split was SK hynix 56.4, Samsung 37.8 and Micron 5.8, which put Korea at 94.2. By the first quarter of 2026 Micron was at 23.1 and Korea was down to 76.9. The figures are IDC's, carried in SK hynix's registered prospectus. China has no HBM production that clears both the export-control thresholds and the performance bar. That gap is the main limit on Huawei's Ascend AI chips. HBM is itself export-controlled, under ECCN 3A090.c, so the segment is unusual in being both extremely concentrated and directly regulated. In HBM4 the base die, the chip at the bottom of the memory stack, is a logic die. That brings TSMC and Samsung Foundry into a segment that used to be pure memory.
trend: Korea's share has fallen from 94.2 percent in 2024 to 82.5 in 2025 and 76.9 in the first quarter of 2026, all of it lost to Micron. The ranking among the three follows which supplier passes customers' qualification tests, and none of the three is Chinese.

method: No shares. No allowed source publishes 2.5D or 3D packaging capacity by country. TSMC's disclosures, SEMI, SIA and ETO's provision table carry advanced-packaging tools (node N109) but no advanced-packaging capacity.
note: The demand side is measured for CoWoS, TSMC's 2.5D packaging process. Epoch AI estimates that Nvidia consumed 60.3 percent of the world's CoWoS capacity in 2025 (90 percent confidence interval 56.5 to 64.3), Google 13.5, AMD 8.4 and Amazon 7.4. It estimates that those four took around 90 percent of all CoWoS and all HBM by value while using about 12 percent of advanced logic die production. That is a split by buyer, and it is the sharpest published measure of how narrow the segment is. Epoch AI builds the estimate on year-end wafers-per-month benchmarks taken from SemiWiki and TrendForce, so the figure is relayed market research, with no institutional measurement behind it. On the supply side, the public record shows which firms rely on which suppliers. Nvidia's annual report states that it uses CoWoS and names TSMC and Samsung as its foundries, and TSMC's CoWoS lines are in Taiwan. In the United States there are Intel's EMIB and Foveros packaging lines in Arizona, Oregon and New Mexico, and the plant Amkor is building in Arizona. In Korea there are Samsung's I-Cube lines and SK hynix's HBM stacking. The capacity is overwhelmingly in Taiwan, and no allowed source measures it.
trend: Advanced packaging was the main limit on AI accelerator output through late 2024 and early 2025. SemiAnalysis reported in March 2026 that the CoWoS shortage had eased and front-end wafer capacity had become the main bottleneck. On TSMC's July 2026 earnings call its chief executive gave a different account, saying packaging capacity was still so tight that it limited customers' growth. Capacity is being added outside Taiwan, but it is small next to TSMC's existing capacity.

method: ATP site capacity by country on a $95bn market in 2022, taken from SIA and carried at stage level (S3) in ETO's provision table. SIA and BCG print the same 2022 split in their 2024 report (Exhibit 2). Columns sum to 99 because of rounding in the source.
note: The figure is four years old, in the segment where country shares have moved most. SIA's 2025 State of the U.S. Semiconductor Industry report carries a 2024 split on the same site-capacity basis: China 28 percent, Taiwan 20, South Korea 9, Japan 8, Europe 7 and an unattributed Other 26, with the US too small to label. The report does not explain Taiwan's fall from 28 to 20 in two years, so the row keeps the 2022 measurement. The merchant assembly and test firms (OSATs) file their own plant lists, but those lists leave out the captive half of the stage, so they cannot supply a denominator. The split is by site. Amkor's plants count in Korea, the Philippines, Vietnam and China and none in the United States, so the US column is 3. The split also counts the assembly and test that integrated device makers (IDMs) and foundries do in-house, alongside the merchant OSATs. That in-house work is most of what Taiwan, Korea and Japan do in this stage. The source does not say which countries make up the 20-point 'various countries' column. SIA and BCG put Southeast Asia, with Malaysia the largest, at about a fifth of global assembly capacity by location in 2022, which is consistent with reading that column as Southeast Asia.
trend: China has the largest single share of assembly and test capacity by site, and it has been adding capacity faster than anyone else. So the export controls reach packaging tools as well as wafer tools.

method: No shares. Both candidate sources name the suppliers without measuring them. Every share field in ETO's Substrates node (N96) is blank. The White House hundred-day supply chain review of June 2021 names the same firms, again with no shares. It lists ABF substrate, built up from Ajinomoto's insulating film, among the materials commenters flagged.
note: ETO's Substrates node lists Ibiden, Shinko, Nan Ya, Samsung, Shennan Circuits, Zhuhai Yueya and AKM against Japan, Korea, Taiwan and China and gives nothing more. The White House review names the same firms the same way. The firms themselves report substrates inside broader electronics segments. So the list of suppliers is the useful part, and it is stable. The suppliers are Unimicron, Nan Ya PCB and Kinsus in Taiwan; Ibiden and Shinko Electric Industries in Japan; Samsung Electro-Mechanics, LG Innotek, Simmtech and Daeduck in Korea; AT&S in Austria; and Shennan Circuits and Zhen Ding in China. There is no US-headquartered volume supplier, as the 2021 review pointed out. The sub-segment used for AI chips is narrower still. The very large, high-layer-count ABF substrates under CoWoS packages come from a handful of Japanese, Taiwanese and Austrian plants. After CoWoS itself, substrates are the constraint most often named. METI said in June 2026 that Japan holds the top share in the high-end package substrates used for AI chips, without giving a figure. AT&S's annual report for 2025/26, citing Prismark, puts the FC-BGA substrate market at $7.5bn in 2025, up 18 percent on 2024. Ibiden gave the one firm-level number on the record, in its investor briefing of May 2026. It says it typically takes close to 100 percent of a new generation of interposer-type substrates at launch and loses 20 to 30 points three to six months later.
trend: Chinese suppliers have grown in mature grades, while Japan and Austria have held the high-layer-count ABF business that AI packages need. No allowed source measures the change.

method: An in-house estimate, because no allowed source publishes AI accelerator silicon as a market with country shares. The US column is built from the design owners' filed revenue. The main inputs are Nvidia's $193,737m of data-center revenue in the year to January 2026, out of $215,938m total, and Broadcom's $63,887m FY2025 total, of which AI silicon is a large and undisclosed part. The Chinese column follows CSIS's work on China replacing imported AI chips with its own.
note: Revenue of AI accelerator silicon attributed to the country of the firm that owns the design. It combines merchant chips, sold to any buyer, and captive chips, designed for one company's own use. US is Nvidia, whose data-center revenue was $193.7bn in the year to January 2026 out of $215.9bn total. The US column also includes AMD's Instinct line, Intel Gaudi, and the custom chips (ASICs) that Broadcom ($63.9bn total revenue FY2025) and Marvell design for Google, Meta, OpenAI and Amazon. Google TPU and AWS Trainium revenue is credited to the US because the design owners are American. But Broadcom, Alchip and MediaTek do much of the physical implementation, the detailed layout work that readies a design for manufacture. Crediting the design-service houses instead would move a few points to TW. CN is Huawei HiSilicon Ascend, Cambricon, Biren, Moore Threads and MetaX.
